nodes.bodyText:
Summary
DRAFT — DO NOT MERGE. This is a negative result, recorded as a PR so the evidence is reviewable.
One slice attempt for the #557 F12.12 p99 criterion, aimed at the input/ack cost in felix's 2026-11-22 profile (PR #12471): after group commit (#8239), durability-before-ack still costs one sync_data per journal append, and at 100 worlds × 20 inputs/s the filesystem's aggregate sync rate was the suspected cap.

nodes.bodyText:
Scope
This draft implements the private, outbound-only laptop bridge for four named Fleet reads: queue status, broker health, laptop health, and bounded diagnostics. Desktop Commander/native Codex remains the fallback. There is no shell, arbitrary filesystem access, generic proxy, or credential capture.
The selected source transport is no-WARP HTTPS to the fixed proposed hostname laptop-bridge-staging.security.cab, protected by Cloudflare Access service authentication and independent Ed25519 request signatures. Worker code requires Cloudflare’s directly authenticated ctx.access.aud to match the configured audience and validates the RS256 Access JWT against the exact issuer, claim audience, hostname, JWKS, signature and time claims. The signed common_name selects one unrevoked principal; x-bridge-principal must name that same principal before forwarding. It does not rely on the original CF-Access-Client-Id request header. Access/cookie/authorization headers are removed before the Durable Object. The hostname, DNS ownership, Access app/policy, and real Node caller/device route are not verified or deployed.
Fixed staging lifecycle and gates
The bridge uses one declared cloudflare.config.ts lifecycle and pinned cf@1.0.0-rc.1. The manual first-deploy template remains at pm-stack/private-laptop-bridge/private-laptop-bridge-staging-bootstrap.workflow.yml.disabled, outside .github/workflows, so it is not registered. It requires an owner-created metadata-only Worker and pinned immutable CF_BRIDGE_WORKER_ID; absent targets and same-name/different-ID takeovers fail closed. It does not grant account-wide Worker creation to Actions. The existing release workflow now checks the exact existing protected cloudflare-staging environment in a no-secret job before environment assignment.
The dormant first-deploy path uses bridge-init: it requires full zone/route inventory, separate Worker and Gateway-rule read identities, an empty deployment/namespace/domain state, disabled worker.dev/previews, exact Worker identity, and absence of any Gateway Forward association. Its postflight requires the disabled source-tagged version and SQLite namespace while verifying zero custom domains and reverse domain references. It does not attach a hostname. The separate routed bridge mode requires protected Access issuer/audience and a later independent Access/domain review. The private owner proof requires the exact Access app, service-token-only policy, no browser/bypass/non-service allow paths, exactly two approved client IDs, and token expirations within one hour. It contains no Client Secrets.
The first deployment template now uses only declarative cf deploy --mode bridge-init --prebuilt --provision, which renders no domain and blank Access issuer/audience. The exact cf --provision behavior on a precreated Worker and the Individual Workers Editor permission required for SQLite initialization have not been independently verified. The workflow is dormant and must remain so until verified. A later hostname attachment path is still not implemented.
Required protected cloudflare-staging configuration

Variables: CF_BRIDGE_WORKER_ID, CF_BRIDGE_BOOTSTRAP_APPROVED_SHA, CF_BRIDGE_ACCESS_ISSUER, and CF_BRIDGE_ACCESS_AUDIENCE.

No values were read, created, or changed. The exact minimum Worker Editor permissions for SQLite namespace provisioning remain a blocker; do not replace them with a Workers-wide credential.

The environment must already exist, require an independent reviewer, disallow self-review/admin bypass, and allow only main. The current checkout does not verify those settings, hostname ownership, Access policy, account zone inventory, or the provider’s first-deploy behavior. Keep the workflow dormant.
Verification status by exact source head

Current candidate: 7f7c2e9317d3ce8e3e44d252f2434d5c6398b526. Exact-head, GitHub-hosted Fleet run 45155722958 asserted this checkout, Node v24.22.0, ran locked npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund, then npm test: 140 passed, 0 failed. nodes.title: id-caps: per-account quota policy and fuel-rate ledger (F12.10 slice 1)
nodes.bodyText:
Refs #1067
Slice
First implementation slice of F12.10 (fair scheduling and per-account quotas). The triage verdicts on #1067 confirmed zero quota/scheduler substrate on main: what exists is per-world ceilings (world_limits: one invocation's fuel, one world's memory), which bound any one world or call but say nothing about an account — one account can still monopolise a hub by spreading work across many worlds or invoking flat-out around the clock.
This slice lands the contract half, in the shape #557 established for the per-world memory budget, in id-caps next to world_limits:

AccountQuotas — validated admin policy: max_worlds, max_storage_bytes, max_fuel_per_second, each nonzero-checked, with proposed-policy defaults (16 worlds, 1 GiB, 100M fuel/s = ten full-budget default invocations per second, sustained).
FuelRateBudget — deterministic fixed-one-second-window ledger with caller-supplied timestamps (no clock reads, no I/O): refuse-whole charges, a typed FuelRateRefusal (distinct from a guest trap and from a per-world ceiling refusal), refusal counting, and a monotone lifetime total for reporting.

Why not enforcement yet
The execution boundary has no account identity today: the world actor and sandbox know worlds and per-invocation fuel, and the hub knows world names, not owning accounts. Wiring the charge into the invocation path requires plumbing world→account ownership to that boundary, which is the next slice (named on #1067) — inventing that mapping inside this PR would be new architecture, not a slice.
Tests

9 new unit tests: default quotas validate; each zero field is rejected; charges accumulate within a window; an over-rate charge is refused whole (atomic, refusal fields, count); the window rolls only after a full second; an idle gap opens a fresh window; an over-limit single charge is refused in a fresh window; an overflowing charge is refused, not wrapped; a policy mints a budget at its own rate.
Full cargo test -p id-caps: 179 passed, 0 failed.
Mutation check: replacing the window-limit comparison with u64::MAX fails 3 of the refusal tests; reverted and re-verified green.

Base is xaltha/id-f1210-account-quota (PR #12539, slice 1) — this slice builds directly on its FuelRateBudget. Retargets to main when #12539 merges.
What
F12.10 slice 2 — the invocation-boundary half of the slice-1 contract. WorldInstance (the sandbox, the one place a guest invocation's fuel is actually set and metered) gains an optional FuelRateBudget:

set_fuel_rate_budget(...) installs the owning account's budget; fuel_rate_budget() exposes it for reporting.

Summary
First slice of #10927 (shells v1 slice 1 — PWA offline read model + catch-up). The browser shell (pkgs/id/web/src/world.ts) held all session state in memory: a reload lost the world entirely, and the reconnect cursor restarted at 0.

New world-snapshot-store.ts: a snapshot store keyed per host + world name, holding {world_id, last applied sequence, participants, rendered view (screen surface or text), view revision, records}. Entries are validated on load with the frame validators' shape discipline (safe non-negative integer sequences/ids, string fields, a surface the renderer accepts); a corrupt or foreign entry is ignored, never rendered and never adopted as the resume cursor. world.ts writes the store through on every snapshot / event / view (full, patched, form) / completed-records frame, and restores it on page load and on a world switch in connect(): participants, view and records render with no socket, the status reads "Offline — saved snapshot" with a read-only log line, and the resume cursor is seeded from the stored sequence so the join frame's after presents the last applied journal sequence across a reload. Offline stays reader-not-writer: the existing send paths refuse without an open socket (covered by test).
Participant badge rendering is extracted into one helper shared by the snapshot handler and the restore path.

Closes #12796
E1 of #9083 (component E, hosted tenancy): the central tenancy DB schema from design §2.1 (doc/2026-11-17T16-55-00Z_design_hosted-tenancy-architecture) lands as a migration baseline in the new control-plane schema home, pkgs/id/hosted-worker/tenancy/.
What

tenancy/migrations/0001_tenancy_baseline.sql — the §2.1 schema as a Turso/SQLite migration: account (identity registry), binding (account→identity/tenant pointer), tenant_db (database registry), role_grant (#1253 vocabulary), peer_policy (#9106/B31 classes as configuration, not a parallel trust model), publish_record, credential (metadata only), plus a meta table carrying schema_version (the user-do.ts bootstrap pattern).
tenancy/README.md — the plane rules, the invariant, and the migration discipline (numbered, append-only; E2/E4/E5 add files here).
test/tenancy-schema.test.ts — guard suite (below), wired into npm test and the id.hosted-worker.routing suite-registry entry.
README.md — a pointer section for the control plane.

Acceptance mapping

Tenancy schema lands as a migration implementing §2.1 — the suite applies the migration to in-memory SQLite and pins the result table-for-table, column-for-column against §2.1.
A test fails if a content/key/token column appears — the never-central guard (§2.3) scans every column of every table against token/key/secret/content-bytes name patterns; a companion test plants violations (token_value, private_key, note_body, blob_bytes, api_secret) and proves the guard bites. Sanctioned references stay legal: content_hash (a content address), iroh_id (the public key), jti (the revocation handle — never the token).
Peer principle honoured — tenant_db.participant_kind is one vocabulary (user_hosted | user_native | self_hosted_node | public) on the shared registry row; a test asserts all four kinds insert identically and no schema object is named for one kind.

Documented statements of the design's rules (migration header)
The design calls its DDL "a sketch for the implementation issues, not a migration"; two spots state the rule rather than the sketch verbatim:

binding: the sketch's UNIQUE (account_id, status) would cap an account at one superseded binding ever, breaking the rebind chain its own superseded_by defines. The stated rule — at most one active row per account — is a partial unique index; the suite walks the full rebind flow (pending → supersede → activate).
Vocabularies the record names as closed carry CHECK constraints: participant_kind, jurisdiction, peer_policy.class, credential.scope. (meta uses name/value columns so the never-central guard needs no exception for it.)

Evidence

New suite: 8/8 pass locally (Node 24, node --experimental-transform-types --test test/tenancy-schema.test.ts).
Full package suite: 44/44 pass (npm test); npm run typecheck clean.
Migration also applied independently under Python sqlite3 3.45.1: 8 tables, schema_version = 1.
check-suite-registry.sh: no violation for the new test file; the 3 violations it reports are the pre-existing #12230 Rust-suite gaps already fixed by open PR #12870.

Coordination
Sibling #12825 (PM tenant store schema) is a different database (the tenant plane) with disjoint tables; this PR touches no PM-store files — footprint is pkgs/id/hosted-worker/tenancy/**, one test file, the package manifest/README, and the registry entry.

Refs #12136 — the guard slice, stacked on PR #13047 (the removal slice). What this adds

.github/scripts/check-root-status-files.sh — fails, naming each offender, when a file at the repository root has a name containing COMPLETE or SUMMARY (case-insensitive). Root only: the same names inside a directory (e.g. the pm-stack/opencode-claimant/ copies) are untouched. Strict one-optional-positional argument contract per #3352.

The repo's ratchet for pre-existing violations is the grandfather list in check-production-line-limit.sh, which exists for violations burned down over many PRs, each entry deleted by the PR that removes the violation. nodes.title: fix(fleet-agent): map oc-* lanes to their family's registered worker
nodes.bodyText:
What
registered_lane_worker in pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-agent/src/next.rs had no mapping for the oc-* scheduled-lane families, so fleet agent next --lane oc-code-02 claimed with --worker oc-code-02 and the broker refused every claim (lane oc-code-02 belongs to worker repo-worker-code, not oc-code-02). The lane starved deterministically.
Fix
Hardcoded mapping, extended in place — the same shape as the existing families (the broker's lane registry is a DB table; this function is the agent-side mirror of its canonical bindings, pinned by the #6853 oracle test, so there is no runtime derivation to extend):

registered_lane_worker strips an oc- prefix and defers to a new oc_lane_worker.
A letter suffix under oc- resolves exactly like the bare lane (oc-not-code-a → not-code-a → repo-worker-nix), by recursion into the existing mapping.
The scheduled lanes' numeric suffix (oc-code-02) resolves by family via a factored-out family_worker (the same family table the bare lanes use): oc-code-*/oc-any-*/oc-not-code-* → repo-worker-code, oc-opencode-* → repo-worker-opencode, oc-openchamber-* → repo-worker-openchamber, oc-nix-* → repo-worker-nix.
An unknown family under oc- still returns None, so the caller falls back to the agent name and the broker's ownership check keeps its say — claim validation is not loosened.

The #6853 oracle table in next_uses_the_registered_worker_for_a_known_lane gains seven oc- rows (numeric per family + the not-code letter variant); each row also asserts the then completion commands carry the registered --worker, which is the issue's acceptance shape.
New next_keeps_the_agent_as_worker_for_an_unknown_oc_lane pins the other direction: oc-bogus-02 claims as the agent, not a registered worker.

nodes.title: feat(atlas-search): D1 hot-cache admission policy — heat, heavy-query, tenant quotas, eviction (#13103)
nodes.bodyText:
Follow-on 3 of 6 under #9134 — the admission policy from §3 and §5 of the D1 tenant hot-cache design (doc/2026-11-23T08-06-00Z_design_atlas_d1_tenant_hot_cache, merged via PR #13098).
What landed
New pure policy module pkgs/atlas-search/worker/src/admission.ts — no imports from the store (follow-on 1, #13100) or the freshness evaluator (follow-on 2, #13101); its entry facts mirror the design §5 schema fields so follow-on 4 (read-path integration) wires it to whatever store lands. Sibling slices were built in parallel from main; this slice does not depend on their branches.

Heat counters — HeatTracker: a key becomes eligible after heatRequests requests inside heatWindowMs (defaults 2 / 10 min). In-memory per isolate; heat is evidence, not state of record.
Heavy-query immediate admission — first request admits when source latency > 250 ms or rows-read > 10,000 (strict inequalities, per the design wording; both are config).
Entry size cap — payloads larger than 256 KB (config) are never admitted, even when heavy or hot.
Negative results — ride the same heat/heavy gates (a single poll is one-hit traffic) and carry the 30 s negative TTL (config) when admitted.
Per-tenant quotas — quotaShares: the 5% floor is reserved per active tenant off the top, the remainder splits by tier weights 1:4:16; if floors alone would exceed the budget (>20 active tenants at the default floor) the whole budget splits by weight instead. Shares always sum to the budget. A tier outside the configured weights is a RangeError, not a silent clamp.
LRU eviction sweep — planEvictions: quota binds only under pressure (database over its total budget); while under budget, unused quota is borrowable and nothing is evicted. Under pressure each over-share tenant sheds least-recently-hit entries, Class B/C before Class A, stopping at its share; a tenant with no share entry sheds everything.

Every threshold is a named AdmissionConfig value with the design's defaults in DEFAULT_ADMISSION_CONFIG — none hardcoded in policy code, per the issue's acceptance.
Also: test/admission.test.ts registered in the atlas-search-worker-tests workflow guard list + header enumeration, and a README shape bullet (noted as not yet wired into the read path).

New suite test/admission.test.ts: 29 tests, 64 assertions, all passing — one or more tests per rule, incl. quota-pressure eviction order, strict heavy thresholds, the window boundary, the floor guarantee, and config-override tests proving thresholds come from config. nodes.title: impl(atlas): D1 hot-cache freshness evaluator — per-class watermark/TTL rules (#13101)
nodes.bodyText:
Follow-on 2 of 6 under #9134 (Atlas D1 tenant hot cache design, merged via PR #13098), implementing §1 + §8 item 2 in pkgs/atlas-search/worker. Based on main — no code dependence on follow-on 1 (#13100, the D1 store).
What landed

src/freshness.ts — the pure freshness evaluator. No I/O, no clock reads: the caller supplies now and the watermark read result.

Class A (content-addressed payloads): the hash is the version — fresh on hash match at any age, watermark state irrelevant; a hash mismatch (or an entry with no hash to prove identity) is never served.
Class B (query result sets): fresh iff the entry's source_watermark still equals the tenant's current watermark and age ≤ TTL_B (default 60 s) — whichever fails first, so a watermark advance is stale even inside the TTL.
Class C (tenant aggregates): fresh iff age ≤ TTL_C (default 15 min) and no invalidation event for the tenant post-dates the entry.
Fail-safe degradation (§1): watermark source unreachable → Class B degrades to TTL-only with TTL_B divided by the degraded divisor (default 2 → 30 s, floored, clamped ≥ 1 so it can never extend), Class C stops being served, Class A unaffected. A future filled_at (clock skew) is never fresh for the TTL classes.
The tenant watermark read: WatermarkSource seam + readTenantWatermark, mapping every source failure (throw, null) to unavailable — unknown can only narrow the bound, never widen it. evaluateWithWatermarkRead composes read + pure evaluation for the read path.
Bounds are named config (ttlBSeconds, ttlCSeconds, degradedDivisor) with the design's defaults; invalid overrides fall back to the defaults.
Verdicts carry a reason (the §2 skip-log surface), the age, the applied bound, and a degraded flag.


test/freshness.test.ts — 23 tests. The named oracle: property tests over generated (watermark, age, class, event) sequences (seeded, reproducible; 200 sequences × up to 12 events across 3 configs) asserting exact agreement with an independent transcription of the §1 table — the stale-serves counter is asserted zero, and so is the over-refusal counter. Plus unit tests for each named rule, config resolution, and the watermark read.
README.md — Shape section gains the module, noting it is not wired into a read path yet (store is #13100, integration is follow-on 4).

Test evidence
The worker package's node_modules are not installed in the sandbox (and installing was out of bounds for this lane), so the committed vitest file was run byte-for-byte under bun test with a vitest→bun:test shim, in a scratch dir outside the repo:

New suite: 23 pass / 0 fail, 1398 expect() calls (the property oracle alone makes >1000 evaluations).
Existing runtime-independent suites (key, body, space): 15 pass / 0 fail under the same shim.
mcp/worker suites import cloudflare:test and need the Cloudflare vitest pool — not runnable in the sandbox; their files are untouched (this PR only adds files plus one README bullet).
Strict typecheck (tsc 5.9.3, --strict --skipLibCheck, package-equivalent flags): both new files pass.
CI (atlas-search-worker-tests) runs the real vitest pool suite and is the first run of the new tests under vitest proper.

Closes #13101

nodes.title: feat(fleet): gh sync verbs for scripted flows (#10973)
nodes.bodyText:
Step 2.2 of #9016 — the Queue/GitHub sync verbs. Refs #10973.
What landed
Eight typed fleet gh sync-* shadow verbs (new module pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/gh_sync.rs): each declares its whole command line, validates it strictly (the #3352 contract — undeclared arguments are usage errors), and rewrites to the canonical gh call. The rewrite is applied in gh::run before the close guard, the closure layer and the metadata create path parse the arguments, so a sync call inherits the step-1 token rotation, the retry-safety rule, value-free errors and the audit trail exactly as the hand-written passthrough call it replaces — and the caller's stdout contract stays gh's own output, byte-exact.



Verb
Canonical call




sync-labels --repo R <issue|pr> N
<kind> view N --json labels --jq [.labels[].name]


sync-view --repo R <issue|pr> N
<kind> view N --json labels,state,title


sync-comment --repo R <issue|pr> N --body T | --body-file P
<kind> comment N --body T (file read by the verb layer; unreadable file refuses before any write)


sync-issue-create --repo R --title T --body … [--label L]…
issue create … (metadata stamping applies downstream)


sync-issue-get --repo R N
api repos/R/issues/N


sync-labels-add --repo R N --label L…
issue edit N --add-label L…


sync-label-ensure --repo R --label L --color C --description D
label create L --force …


sync-issue-close --repo R N --reason <fleet reason>
issue close N --reason <fleet reason> (closure layer appends the reason comment + record)



Registry help inventory (fleet-registry) and pkgs/fleet/docs/verbs.md updated in the same change.
Caller evidence

pm-stack/opencode-claimant/claimant.py — the label read now runs sync-labels (same fail-closed contract, #7670); the three agent-note posts (launch / hand-back / stuck-holder) were deduplicated into one helper over sync-comment. No raw gh composition remains in the file.
pm-stack/opencode-claimant/launch_one.py — the hard-stop read runs sync-view; the launch note post runs sync-comment --body-file (it already staged the note to a file). Its callers in send_to_opencode.py inherit both.
pm-stack/dispatch/src/github.ts — the whole gh fallback route runs through the packaged fleet binary (PM_DISPATCH_FLEET_BIN, default ~/.local/bin/fleet, the claimant's packaged location): ensureLabel → sync-label-ensure, createIssue → sync-issue-create, getIssue → sync-issue-get, addLabels → sync-labels-add, closeIssue → sync-issue-close, comment → sync-comment. The pm-stack App REST route stays primary and untouched. Disclosure: the verb close speaks the fleet closure taxonomy (#9221), so dispatch's not_planned maps to cancelled and completed to implemented; GitHub's own state_reason granularity is not preserved. Every live caller closes with not_planned, compensating a dispatch-created tracking issue whose launch failed (launch_failure.ts).
Job-body flows (program tending, stewardship verdict posting, pool reviews) — their GitHub operations are the same two shapes these verbs cover (comment posts, label/state reads). Their bodies live outside this repo, so they adopt the verbs from their own definitions; that adoption is the remaining acceptance item, which is why this PR says Refs, not Closes.

Overlap with step 2.1 (#10972)
Built independently from main, per the sequencing: no dependency on the 2.1 branch. Both steps need strict verb parsing; here it lives inside gh_sync.rs as a small declared-flags parser. If 2.1 lands its own, factoring a shared helper is a small follow-up either way.
